post.description:
Create a Machine within a specific app using the details provided in the request body.

**Important**: This request can fail, and you’re responsible for handling that failure. If you ask for a large Machine, or a Machine in a region we happen to be at capacity for, you might need to retry the request, or to fall back to another region. If you’re working directly with the Machines API, you’re taking some responsibility for your own orchestration!

delete.description:
Delete a specific Machine within an app by Machine ID.

Only a Machine in the `stopped`, `suspended`, `failed`, `pending` or `archived` state can be deleted. Deleting a Machine in any other state, such as `started`, fails with `412 Precondition Failed` unless you set `force=true`, which kills the Machine first. Deleting a Machine that is already `destroying` or `destroyed` succeeds without doing anything.

If someone else holds a lease on the Machine, the request fails with `409 Conflict`. Pass the lease nonce in the `fly-machine-lease-nonce` header to delete a Machine you hold the lease on.

parameters.name: force
parameters.description: Kill the Machine first if it's not stopped, suspended, failed, pending or archived

409.description: Another client holds a lease on the Machine

412.description: The Machine isn't stopped, suspended, failed, pending or archived, and force isn't set

post.description: “Cordoning” a Machine refers to disabling its services, so the Fly Proxy won’t route requests to it. In flyctl this is used by blue/green deployments; one set of Machines is started up with services disabled, and when they are all healthy, the services are enabled on the new Machines and disabled on the old ones.

post.description:
Execute a command on a specific Machine and return a JSON response containing
stdout, stderr, exit_code, and exit_signal.

A completed command returns HTTP 200, including when the command exits
unsuccessfully.

HTTP 412 is returned when the Machine is not running. On Machines without
containers, it can also indicate an error before or during command execution.
For example, the executable may be missing or lack execute permission. The
`error` field describes the failure.

HTTP 413 responses include a `status` field identifying the size limit that was
exceeded:

* `exec_request_too_large`: the Machine rejected the exec request as too large.
  The error message is `exec request rejected: payload too large`. The limit
  applies to the encoded request sent to the Machine, which can differ in size
  from the public API request.
* `exec_output_too_large`: the command ran, but its output could not be returned
  because it exceeded the maximum allowed response size after JSON encoding.

412.description: An error occurred before or during command execution

413.description: Size limit exceeded; status is exec_request_too_large or exec_output_too_large

get.description: Get the current memory limit of a started Firecracker Machine, and how far it can be raised.

put.description:
Set the memory limit of a started Firecracker Machine by resizing its memory balloon. The limit lasts until the Machine stops or is updated.
+ Fails with 409 while the Machine has a lease, even when the lease nonce is passed.

400.description: limit_mb is below 128 or above the Machine's memory.

412.description: The Machine is not started, or does not run on Firecracker.

429.description: The host does not have enough free memory to raise the limit.

post.description:
Return unused memory of a started Firecracker Machine to the host. The memory balloon is inflated by `amount_mb` for a few seconds and then deflated again, so the Machine's memory limit does not change.
+ Fails with 409 while the Machine has a lease, even when the lease nonce is passed.

400.description: amount_mb is not positive, or exceeds the Machine's memory limit minus 128 MiB.

412.description: The Machine is not started, or does not run on Firecracker.

get.description:
List all Machines associated with a specific organization. Machines are returned region by region, and sorted by their `updated_at` timestamps, oldest to newest, within each region. The list as a whole is therefore not sorted by `updated_at`.

This API call represents "a point in time". Recent machine changes, including creations and destructions, may take time to propagate. When polling with `updated_after`, offset your timestamps to catch late-arriving events.

parameters.description: Comma separated list of states to filter (created, started, stopped, suspended)

parameters.name: updated_after
parameters.description: Only return machines updated after this time. Timestamp must be in the RFC 3339 format

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: Pagination cursor from previous response (takes precedence over updated_after). Note that there is no guarantee that all machines returned by this endpoint are sorted by their updated_at fields. Pagination may reveal machines older than the last updated_at.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: The number of machines to fetch (max of 1000). This limit is advisory. Responses may be shorter, or even empty, even when more machines remain. If omitted, the maximum is used

it. Keys and values have surrounding whitespace trimmed. Keys not listed are left alone.
